mech: Pollen and lagoon cores show a 150-year dry spell that cut harvests on the Anatolian plateau, the most rain-dependent of the great kingdoms.
Juniper rings from Gordion show three consecutive very dry years around 1198-1196 BCE, just before Hattusa was abandoned.
A kingdom that had to import grain by sea could not feed its capital and army once Ugarit and the shipping lanes failed.
The fall of the Hittite overlord removed the power that policed Syria and western Anatolia, so vassals like Ugarit stood alone.
Dry centuries shrank the grain surplus that fed palaces, armies and trade from Cyprus to Syria; the destruction layers sit on top of the dry phase.
Hungry Aegean and Anatolian populations took to the sea in search of land and food.
Ugarit's last letters report enemy ships burning its towns while its own fleet and army were away in Hittite service.

view: Ramesses III's inscriptions as read by Cline
mech: The coalition that had swept the coast reached the Nile and fought Egypt by land and sea.
Waves of migrating warriors overran the coastal kingdoms; the collapse was an invasion.
Many sites blamed on the Sea Peoples show no destruction at all, or burned in accidents or earthquakes; raiders were a symptom, not the engine.
Egypt won its battles but spent its strength; within a generation it pulled out of Canaan and Philistines settled the coast.
Crushed skeletons and tilted walls at Mycenae, Tiryns and Midea point to earthquakes, which may have finished off stressed palaces.
A cluster of quakes over decades would knock down several centres at once and stretch every kingdom's resources.
Once massed barbarian foot soldiers learned to kill chariot horses and crews, the palace armies lost the edge that kept them in power.
Raiders with Naue II swords and javelins sacked palaces whose defence rested on chariots.
Kingdoms that depended on each other for copper, tin, grain and gifts passed every shock along the network, so one failure became many.
Linear B was a palace accounting script; when the palaces burned, nobody needed or taught it.
Without palaces and long-distance trade, Greece fell back on small farming villages and its population shrank for generations.
The palaces' end was a political collapse of a thin elite; many communities carried on, moved, or reorganised rather than vanishing.
With palace scribes and their complex scripts gone, merchant cities spread a 22-letter alphabet anyone could learn.

view: Snodgrass's tin-shortage thesis, as weighed by Dickinson
mech: Broken trade routes cut the tin needed for bronze, pushing smiths to local iron ore.
With the palaces gone, Cypriot towns and merchants took over the copper trade on their own account.
The vacuum left by Hatti, Egypt and the Mitanni let a surviving Assyria rebuild and expand into a world without rivals.
The cold, dry snap shrank wild cereal stands around settled Natufian hamlets, so people began to plant what they could no longer gather.
Ice Age climate swung too wildly from decade to decade for farming to pay; the stable, CO2-richer Holocene made it possible and then, in competition, unavoidable.
Farming appeared independently in several regions within a few thousand years of the Holocene's start, which points to a global trigger.
Sharper seasons at the end of the Pleistocene rewarded people who stored food for the lean months, and storing seed led to sowing it.
Settled villages let populations grow and strip local wild stands, so cultivation became the way to keep living in one place.
Foragers everywhere had filled their landscapes by the end of the Ice Age; farming was a reluctant way to get more calories per acre.
Stored grain and fixed homes made private property enforceable, and property let farming spread even though early farming was barely more productive than foraging.
Feasts at monumental gatherings demanded grain for bread and beer; ambitious hosts had reason to cultivate.
Centuries of harvesting and sowing selected wheat whose ears no longer shattered, a slow niche-building process, not an overnight invention.
Starchy cereal diets, crowded villages and animals living close by brought cavities, anaemia and new infections.

view: Clark Spencer Larsen; James C. Scott
mech: Sedentary mothers with cereal porridge could wean earlier and have more children, so farmers outbred foragers despite worse health.

view: James C. Scott; Mayshar, Moav & Pascali
mech: Cereals ripen at once, can be measured and stored, and are easy to tax; states grew where grain, not tubers, was the staple.
Farming came about 6,000 years before the first state; in between, people tried many social forms, so farming did not lead to states by itself.
Large populations organised themselves into towns of thousands without kings, showing that scale does not require a state.
Big canal systems needed central managers, and the managers became despots. Archaeology later found the canals were small and local until long after states existed.
Irrigated alluvium produced a surplus that could feed full-time priests, craftsmen and officials, the core of an urban revolution.
Temple institutions and inherited rank came first; kingship grew out of the ritual authority of hereditary elites.
In a valley walled by desert, losers could not flee; war turned them into subjects and villages into one kingdom.
The earliest tablets are ration lists, labour accounts and tallies of grain and sheep: writing was invented to run the state's storehouse.
A resource-poor alluvium with good river transport sent colonists upstream to secure timber, metal and stone.
Once people in the new Ganges cities lived well above subsistence, teachings of self-control and detachment from desire found an audience.
The same urban, monetised world of the Ganges plain produced the ascetic teaching of Mahavira.
Rising energy capture in north China made long-term, self-disciplined strategies of life pay, and moral philosophies spread.
The Daodejing's praise of contentment and few desires answers a society suddenly rich enough to want more.
Prosperous Greek cities produced philosophies of moderation and the soul's discipline.
Coins made a single abstract value stand behind many things; Greek thinkers began to see the world as one invisible substance behind appearances.
Coins, professional armies and slave markets arose together in Greece, India and China, and the new philosophies were reactions to that market world.
Mass armies paid in coin spread markets and debt across China; sages from Confucius to Mozi argued against a world of profit.
Two and a half thousand years of literate states let people step back and argue about ideas in writing: the move from myth to theory.
Moralizing ideals of justice tied to kingship appeared with the first large states, not in one later age; the Seshat data show them tracking scale, not date.
If moral religion appeared in Egypt and Mesopotamia long before 800 BCE, the 'Axial Age' is a regional crest, not a worldwide break.

view: Staubwasser et al.; Dixit, Hodell & Petrie
mech: An abrupt weakening of the summer monsoon around 4,200 to 4,100 years ago cut the rains and floods that Harappan farming relied on.
Villages in northwest India already grew both summer and winter crops on uneven rainfall; the drought tested them but rural life went on, so the link is weak.
The Ghaggar-Hakra was fed by monsoon rain, not glaciers; as the rains faded, so did its floods.
Farmers left the drying plains for the Himalayan foothills and the Ganges-Yamuna doab, where rain was steadier.
Winter rains held up in the northeast while the summer monsoon failed in the west, so settlement followed the water east.
When people dispersed into small villages, the cities and the shared system of weights, seals and script lost their reason to exist: a transformation, not an extinction.
The fall of Ur and Mesopotamian upheaval cut the demand for carnelian, ivory and timber that the Gulf trade had served.
Urban elites who controlled long-distance trade lost the exotic goods and profits that marked their status.
As the climate and the economy worsened, injuries and infectious disease rose, especially among people buried apart from the community.
Rising violence and exclusion show a social order coming apart from within, not a peaceful fade.
Wheeler blamed chariot-riding Aryans for a massacre at Mohenjo-daro ('Indra stands accused'); the skeletons come from different levels and periods, and steppe ancestry arrives after the decline.
People of Indus ancestry who moved north and east after the cities emptied mixed with incoming steppe groups to form the Ancestral North Indians.
Abandonment of the rain-fed Habur plains at the start of the 4.2 ka drought broke the grain base of the Akkadian empire.
Low Nile floods may have stressed a state that was already splitting into provincial power centres; the timing fits, the mechanism is unproven.
Warm, wet and stable weather around the Mediterranean raised harvests and let the population grow to its imperial peak.
Lead pollution from Roman silver mining drops in the Greenland ice in the 160s, just when the plague struck, and does not recover until the Middle Ages.
A first pandemic killed perhaps a tenth or more of the empire and drained the army and treasury that later emergencies needed.
In Egypt the plague hit villages already hurt by bad floods, and the damage was local and uneven rather than empire-wide.
Drought and weak Nile floods in the 240s struck an empire already short of men and money.
A second pandemic in the 250s came as the frontiers broke; the empire nearly dissolved into three pieces.
Christians nursed the sick and buried the dead when others fled, and the church grew in the plague years.
Emperors facing constant wars paid soldiers in ever thinner silver until the coinage was almost bronze.
Fifty years of usurpations and invasions convinced Diocletian to multiply emperors, provinces and soldiers.
With silver discredited, the state switched to a heavy gold coin and collected taxes in gold or in kind.
A bigger army and bureaucracy bought survival at rising cost; taxes drove peasants off marginal land and each new crisis bought less security.
The Huns' arrival north of the Black Sea broke the Gothic kingdoms there and drove the Tervingi and Greuthungi to the Danube.
Roman officers let the refugees starve and sold them dogs for their children; the Goths revolted and destroyed Valens' army.
Unable to destroy the Goths after losing two-thirds of an army, Theodosius had to settle them as an autonomous people inside the empire.
A Gothic army that kept its own leaders became Alaric's bargaining weapon, and when Rome would not pay, he sacked it.
Alaric wanted a Roman generalship and pay; the sack followed the execution of Stilicho and Honorius' refusal to deal, a failure of Roman politics.
As the Huns moved onto the Hungarian plain, the peoples in their path were pushed west over the upper Danube and the Rhine.
Stilicho stripped the frontier for his wars with Alaric and the East, and Roman political crisis drew barbarians in rather than barbarians breaking it.
Years of armies marching through Gaul and Spain wrecked the tax registers of the West's second and third richest regions.
Settled barbarians were paid with shares of tax revenue, not stolen land: accommodation kept the peace but quietly shifted the fisc away from the emperor.
Africa was the West's richest remaining province and Rome's bread basket; its loss cut revenue and the army that revenue paid for.
Retaking Africa was the only way to restore Western finances, so East and West gambled on a vast joint fleet.
The armada's destruction bankrupted the effort; after 468 nobody could pay a Western army big enough to matter.
No taxes, no army: by the 470s the emperor in Italy was a figurehead for whichever general controlled the last troops.
Romans fought Romans far more often than they fought barbarians; each usurpation pulled troops from the frontier and invited outsiders in as allies.
The third century taught the army that it could make emperors; the habit of usurpation never went away.
Two courts under boy emperors bred rival favourites who betrayed each other; Constantinople watched the West's disasters with indifference.
Gibbon said the church preached patience and drew talent and wealth into the cloister; but the more Christian East survived, which sinks the argument.
Without the state's army, taxes and roads, specialised production and long-distance trade collapsed; pottery, coin and even cattle shrank.
Holy men, bishops and monasteries created new centres of power and culture, so the period reads as transformation as much as fall.
The volcanic winters of 536-540 and the cold that followed came just before plague arrived; cold and hunger may have helped rodents and fleas spread it.
A century of cold summers coincided with Avar and Slavic movements into the Balkans.
Plague cut the manpower and taxpayers Justinian needed to hold reconquered Italy.
Papyri, laws, coin finds and pollen show little sign of an empire-breaking die-off; the plague may have been far less consequential.
Belisarius' small army took Carthage in 533 and ended the Vandal kingdom within a year.
Two decades of war in Italy destroyed the Ostrogothic kingdom and much of Italy with it.
Italy came out of the Gothic war exhausted and lightly garrisoned, an easy target for the next invaders.
A surplus of gold from Egypt and the East funded fleets and armies to reconquer Africa and Italy.
Water on three sides and a land front of about 6 km, with control of the straits between Europe and Asia.
A triple line of moat, outer and inner walls with almost 100 towers that no army without a fleet and siege train could break.
Huge cisterns inside the walls stored water brought from the Thracian hills, so a city of hundreds of thousands could ride out a siege even when the aqueduct was cut.
The East's tax base was richer and safe behind the straits, so it could rebuild armies after every defeat; the West's rich provinces were the ones overrun.
Only a treasury that kept collecting Egyptian and Syrian taxes could afford thousands of pounds of gold for Attila.
Hunnic raids through the Balkans in the 440s forced Constantinople to buy peace on Attila's terms.
With the Balkans stripped and the new emperor Marcian refusing to pay, Attila turned to the richer, weaker West.
Attila's campaigns in Gaul (451) and Italy (452) wrecked more of the West's remaining tax base.
Paying gold, which taxes could replace, instead of losing armies, which could not be replaced, was the core of Byzantine strategy.
With Persia mostly at peace for a century, the East could face the Huns and Goths on one front.
The Eastern emperor kept control of the army; no barbarian generalissimo like Ricimer ever made and unmade emperors in Constantinople.
Zeno sent Theodoric's Goths to take Italy from Odoacer, exporting the Balkans' biggest problem west.
A permanent capital where emperor, senate and people met made the city itself the Roman republic; emperors fell, but the polity held.
A codified law and a salaried, literate bureaucracy kept taxes flowing whoever sat on the throne.
Because the capital and its fiscal machine survived the seventh-century disasters, the state could reorganise its armies instead of dissolving.
Persian armies overran Syria and Palestine and then took Egypt, the empire's granary.
Without Egyptian revenues the state could not pay its armies in cash and had to support them from the land.
A quarter century of war left both empires exhausted just as the Arab armies came out of Arabia.
After losing Syria the field armies fell back to Anatolia and were quartered on districts that became the themes.
Tenants on the estates of great families vanished from the tax and labour registers.
Repeated campaigns in the northwest consumed billions of cash and led the court to abandon whole commanderies.
Under Tanshihuai the Xianbei raided the northern frontier almost yearly, and a failed Han offensive in 177 wasted an army.
A court unable to fund relief or garrisons left the eastern plain to floods, famine and local strongmen.
Purging the reformist gentry cut the court off from the provincial elites who held local order together.
The Way of Great Peace healed by confession and charmed water; repeated epidemics brought it hundreds of thousands of followers.
Colder, drier decades would have cut harvests on the north China plain; the case rests on coarse proxies.
To crush the rebels the court armed generals and provincial governors, who then had armies of their own.
The feud between eunuchs and officials ended in the palace massacre of 189, which let Dong Zhuo's frontier troops walk into the capital.
After 190 the emperor was a hostage of warlords; from 196 Cao Cao ruled in his name until his son took the throne.
Grain from the military colonies let Cao Cao unite the north and launch his southern campaign of 208.
Defeat on the Yangzi ended Cao Cao's hope of reuniting China and left room for Liu Bei and Sun Quan.
Once Cao Pi took the throne, Liu Bei and later Sun Quan declared their own dynasties.
The great families and their armed dependants became the building blocks of the warlord regimes and the three kingdoms.
After 280 Jin disarmed the provincial forces and gave armies to imperial princes, who tore the dynasty apart and opened the north to Xiongnu generals.
The pike phalanx held the line while the Companion cavalry struck at the king himself.
A professional army trained by Philip beat a larger royal army on ground Darius had chosen.
Persian roads, depots and river crossings let the Macedonians feed themselves deep inside the empire.

view: Greek sources and the older 'decadence' model
mech: Palace murders supposedly left a decadent empire with a weak king; Achaemenid specialists reject the picture as Greek propaganda.
With the royal army broken, Babylon and Susa opened their gates and the empire's heartland fell in weeks.
A king who had fled two battles lost the loyalty of his satraps, who seized him to bargain or rule themselves.
With Darius dead, Alexander could claim to avenge him and inherit the throne.
The victory opened the road to Persepolis, where Alexander burned the palace against Parmenio's advice.
The hoards of Susa and Persepolis, saved over two centuries, were loaded onto pack animals and turned into coin to pay soldiers.
Persian silver paid the mercenary armies that Alexander's generals threw at each other for forty years.
Alexander died at 32 without an adult heir, and his generals fought for the pieces.
Seleucus emerged with Babylonia and most of the old Persian east.
Alexander was 'the last of the Achaemenids': the Seleucids ruled with Persian satrapies, roads, tribute and royal ideology.
To hold an empire twenty times bigger than Macedon, Alexander needed the Persian nobles and their system.
Iron tools and weapons made at Meroe supported farming and the army of the southern kingdom; the old 'Birmingham of Africa' label overstated its scale.
The treaty of Samos fixed a frontier and lifted tribute, opening two and a half centuries of trade with Roman Egypt.
When Roman Egypt's economy sank in the third century, the Nile trade that enriched Meroe's court dried up.
Roman ships sailing the monsoon to India called at Adulis, where Aksum sold ivory from the interior.
Ivory and exotic goods that once went down the Nile through Meroe now went to the Red Sea through Aksum.
A state trading with Rome and India struck gold coins with Greek legends for use overseas.
Ezana boasts of crushing the Noba and Kasu on the Nile; whether he toppled Meroe or picked over its ruins is argued.
The Meroitic state faded as new Noba-related groups took over the riverine heartland; the change was regional and gradual.
As a Christian kingdom allied to Constantinople, Aksum intervened to avenge the Christians of Najran and control the Red Sea crossing.
Overseas rule in Yemen ended with a breakaway general and then Persian conquest around 570, leaving Aksum shut out of Arabia.
The Arab conquest of Egypt and the shift of trade to Muslim ports and Gulf routes cut Adulis out of the Mediterranean-India traffic.
Centuries of farming and wood-cutting stripped the slopes around the capital, and weaker rains finished the job.
The evidence for catastrophic erosion is thin; the kingdom shifted south and changed rather than collapsing from soil loss.
